citation.title: Sharp bounds on the variance in randomized experiments

standing_assumptions: [Population and design: Section 2, p. 851 (PDF p. 2)] Consider a population $U_N$ consisting of $N \ge 4$ units. From $U_N$, $n$ units are randomly sampled into the experimental sample, and the remaining $N - n$ units are left unsampled. Of the $n$ sampled units, $m \ge 2$ units are randomly assigned to the treatment condition, and $n - m \ge 2$ units are randomly assigned to the control condition. Let the indicator variable $X_i^T$ be one if unit $i$ is assigned to the treatment condition, and let the indicator $X_i^C$ be one if unit $i$ is assigned to the control condition. If $X_i^T = X_i^C = 0$, then the unit is unsampled. Since units are sampled without replacement, $X_i^T + X_i^C \le 1$. Without loss of generality, assume an index ordering $i = 1, \ldots, N$ such that those assigned to treatment come first, $X_1^T, \ldots, X_m^T = 1$, and those assigned to control come after, $X_{m+1}^C, \ldots, X_n^C = 1$, and the remaining $N - n$ unsampled units, if any, come last. Associated with each unit $i$ are two potential outcomes [13, 15] under control and treatment, respectively: $y_{0i}$ and $y_{1i}$. For each unit $i$, the analyst then observes $y_{0i}$ when $X_i^C = 1$ and $y_{1i}$ when $X_i^T = 1$. Given elements $v_i, w_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, N$, we define the finite population mean $\mu_N(v)$, finite population variance $\sigma_N^2(v)$ and finite population covariance $\sigma_N(v, w)$, respectively, as $\mu_N(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N v_i$, $\sigma_N^2(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\{v_i - \mu_N(v)\}^2$, $\sigma_N(v, w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\{v_i - \mu_N(v)\}\{w_i - \mu_N(w)\}$. The average treatment effect for the population $U_N$ is $\tau_N = \mu_N(y_1) - \mu_N(y_0)$. The difference-in-means estimator of $\tau_N$ is (1) $\hat\tau_N = \hat\mu_N(y_1) - \hat\mu_N(y_0) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m y_{1i} - \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=m+1}^n y_{0i}$, with $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat\tau_N) = \tau_N$, where the expectation operator $\mathrm{E}_X$ averages over all $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ possible treatment assignments. Our inferential target is the variance of $\hat\tau_N$. Adapting Freedman [3], Proposition 1, the variance is (2) $V_N = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Reading: the potential outcomes are deterministic (p. 850: 'a nonparametric model of deterministic potential outcomes'); the only randomness is the assignment, the $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ assignments being equally likely; $\mathrm{E}_X$, $\mathrm{Var}_X$ and $\mathrm{P}$ refer to it.] [Marginal variance estimators: p. 852 (PDF p. 3)] By Cochran [1], Theorem 2.4, unbiased estimators of $\sigma_N^2(y_1)$ and $\sigma_N^2(y_0)$ are $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) = \frac{N-1}{N(m-1)}\sum_{i=1}^m\{y_{1i} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\}^2$, $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) = \frac{N-1}{N(n-m-1)}\sum_{i=m+1}^n\{y_{0i} - \hat\mu_N(y_0)\}^2$. [The case $n = N$: Section 2.1, pp. 852–853 (PDF pp. 3–4)] When $n = N$, the sampling variance of the difference-in-means estimator reduces to (3) $V_n = \frac{1}{n-1}\left\{\frac{n-m}{m}\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \frac{m}{n-m}\sigma_n^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_n(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. (4) $\hat V_n^a = \frac{n}{n-1}\left\{\frac{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)}{m} + \frac{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)}{n-m}\right\}$. (5) $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat V_n^a - V_n) = (n-1)^{-1}\{\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \sigma_n^2(y_0) - 2\sigma_n(y_1, y_0)\} \ge 0$. (6) $\hat V_n^{b\pm} = \frac{1}{n-1}\left[\frac{n-m}{m}\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \frac{m}{n-m}\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0) \pm 2\{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)\}^{1/2}\right]$. [Marginal distributions and sharp bounds: Section 3, p. 853 (PDF p. 4)] Let $G_N(y) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{1i} \le y)$ and $F_N(y) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{0i} \le y)$ be the marginal distribution functions of $y_1$ and $y_0$, respectively. Define their left-continuous inverses as $G_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : G_N(y) \ge u\}$ and $F_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : F_N(y) \ge u\}$. Define also (7) $\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(u)\,du - \mu_N(y_1)\mu_N(y_0)$, $\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du - \mu_N(y_1)\mu_N(y_0)$. [p. 853] $V_N^H = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)\right\}$, $V_N^L = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Estimators: p. 854 (PDF p. 5)] In practice, we observe neither $G_N$ nor $F_N$, but rather their estimates $\hat G_N(y) = m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^T I(y_{1i} \le y)$, $\hat F_N(y) = (n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^C I(y_{0i} \le y)$ and left-continuous inverses $\hat G_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : \hat G_N(y) \ge u\} = y_{1(\lceil mu\rceil)}$, $\hat F_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : \hat F_N(y) \ge u\} = y_{0(m+\lceil (n-m)u\rceil)}$, where $y_{1(1)} \le \cdots \le y_{1(m)}$ and $y_{0(m+1)} \le \cdots \le y_{0(n)}$ are the ordered observed outcomes, and $\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$. Substituting $(\hat G_N, \hat F_N)$ for $(G_N, F_N)$ in (7) yields an interval estimator $[\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0), \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)]$ for $\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)$: $\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 \hat G_N^{-1}(u)\hat F_N^{-1}(u)\,du - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, $\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 \hat G_N^{-1}(u)\hat F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$. Let the $[0, 1]$-partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n} = \{p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_P\}$ be the ordered distinct elements of $\{0, 1/m, 2/m, \ldots, 1\} \cup \{0, 1/(n-m), 2/(n-m), \ldots, 1\}$. Let $y_{1[i]} = y_{1(\lceil mp_i\rceil)}$ and $y_{0[i]} = y_{0\{m+\lceil (n-m)p_i\rceil\}}$. The inverses $\hat G_N^{-1}$ and $\hat F_N^{-1}$ are piecewise constant since $\hat G_N^{-1}(u) = y_{1[i]}$ and $\hat F_N^{-1}(u) = y_{0[i]}$ for $u \in (p_{i-1}, p_i]$. In addition, the symmetry $p_i = 1 - p_{P-i}$ implies that $p_i - p_{i-1} = p_{P+1-i} - p_{P-i}$. Thus, $[\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0), \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)]$ reduces to (8) $\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \sum_{i=1}^P (p_i - p_{i-1})y_{1[i]}y_{0[i]} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, $\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \sum_{i=1}^P (p_i - p_{i-1})y_{1[i]}y_{0[P+1-i]} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, where $\hat\mu_N(y_1)$ and $\hat\mu_N(y_0)$ are as defined in (1). Substituting $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1)$, $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0)$, and (8) for $\{\sigma_N^2(y_1), \sigma_N^2(y_0), \sigma_N(y_1, y_0)\}$ in the expressions for $V_N^L$ and $V_N^H$, we obtain the interval estimator $[\hat V_N^L, \hat V_N^H]$ for $V_N$: (9) $\hat V_N^H = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)\right\}$, $\hat V_N^L = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Asymptotic setting: Section 4, p. 855 (PDF p. 6)] Let $\{U_N\}_N$ be a nested sequence of finite populations. The potential outcomes $y_1$ and $y_0$ of each unit are fixed, and hence the population grows deterministically. As in Isaki and Fuller [10], we do not assume that the sequences of treatment assignments are nested; instead, each $U_N$ hosts its own random assignment. Let $H_N(\cdot, \cdot)$ be the joint distribution function of $(y_1, y_0)$ for $U_N$. [Conditions of Proposition 1, p. 855 (PDF p. 6), 'as $N \to \infty$'] 1. $(m/N, n/N) \to (\theta\rho, \theta)$ for $\theta \in (0, 1]$ and $\rho \in (0, 1)$; 2. $H_N$ converges weakly to a limit distribution $H$ with marginals $G(y) = H(y, \infty)$ and $F(y) = H(\infty, y)$; 3. $G_N(y) \to G(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $G$, and $F_N(y) \to F(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $F$; 4. The sequences of distributions represented by $\{G_N\}_N$ and $\{F_N\}_N$ are uniformly square-integrable. That is, as $\beta \to \infty$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i : y_{1i}^2 \ge \beta} y_{1i}^2\right\}$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i : y_{0i}^2 \ge \beta} y_{0i}^2\right\} \to 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, 'a 7% reduction in the nominal variance' (with Table 1), corrected claim
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 857 (PDF p. 8)] Compared to the conventional variance estimator $\hat V_N^a$, we find that our upper bound estimator yields a 7% reduction in the nominal variance. [Table 1, p. 857 (PDF p. 8); columns: Variance estimate (USD$^2$); 95% confidence interval for $\tau_N$] Conventional ($\hat V_N^a$): 0.199; $(-\$1.555, \$0.192)$. Neyman upper bound ($\hat V_N^{b+}$): 0.196; $(-\$1.548, \$0.185)$. Neyman lower bound ($\hat V_N^{b-}$): 0.003; N/A. Sharp upper bound ($\hat V_N^H$): 0.186; $(-\$1.528, \$0.165)$. Sharp lower bound ($\hat V_N^L$): 0.098; N/A. [Corrected claim, from Sol's smallest repair] '… we find that our upper bound estimator yields about a 6% reduction in the nominal variance.' [Formal content] Say that a real number $x$ displays as the three-decimal number $p$ if $p - \frac{1}{2000} \le x \le p + \frac{1}{2000}$ (closed bins, so every round-to-nearest tie rule is allowed). Let $V_a, V_H > 0$ be the conventional and the sharp upper bound variance estimates, let the two intervals be Wald intervals with a common critical value $z > 0$, so that their half-widths are $a = z\sqrt{V_a}$ and $h = z\sqrt{V_H}$ and $V_H/V_a = (h/a)^2$, and let $D = 100(1 - V_H/V_a)$ be the percentage reduction. (a) If the endpoints of the conventional interval display as $-1.555$ and $0.192$ and those of the sharp interval as $-1.528$ and $0.165$, then $0.873 \le a \le 0.874$, $0.846 \le h \le 0.847$ and $D \le 100\left\{1 - \left(\frac{423}{437}\right)^2\right\} = \frac{1204000}{190969} < \frac{13}{2}$: the reduction cannot round to 7%. (b) If in addition $V_a$ displays as $0.199$ and $V_H$ displays as $0.186$, then $D \ge 100\left(1 - \frac{1865}{1985}\right) = \frac{2400}{397} > \frac{11}{2}$. Hence $\frac{2400}{397} \le D \le \frac{1204000}{190969}$ (about $6.045 \le D \le 6.305$), and $D$ rounds to 6%. (c) The printed 7% is what the displayed variances give when treated as exact: $100\left(1 - \frac{0.186}{0.199}\right) = \frac{1300}{199} \approx 6.53$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Remark 4, p. 857 (PDF p. 8)] a confidence interval constructed as $\hat\tau_N \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}$. The Table 1 intervals are read as this Wald construction applied to each variance estimate with one critical value; the value of $z$ and the centre cancel. 'Reduction in the nominal variance' compared to $\hat V_N^a$ is read as $100(1 - \hat V_N^H/\hat V_N^a)$. [p. 857] $N = n = 1561$, $m = 781$. No other object of the paper is needed; the statement concerns the printed numbers only.
canonical_claim.note: P022-N003 is rated an error, Minor. It is a finding about a reported number, included because its entire content is an exact arithmetic impossibility; the corrected figure is the validator's ('a 6% reduction' or 'about a 6% reduction'). The validator already holds a Lean certificate of (a) from the hypotheses $a > 0$, $a \le 437/500$, $h \ge 423/500$ (validate/P022-N003/v1/artifact/check.lean, with lean-output.txt), which the formalizer may restate in the project namespace. Not established: the exact unrounded reduction (the application data are unavailable) or the procedure that produced 7%. The two columns of Table 1 are not themselves inconsistent (the derivation gives a witness). The neighbouring statements 'over 100 additional subjects' and 'over 75 additional subjects' hold under the same reading (at least $100.4$ and $75.3$) and are not targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.1, Sharp Null: the bias '($-0.007$ USD$^2$)' of $\hat V_N^{b+}$ (with Table 2), corrected claim
canonical_claim.location: p. 858 (PDF p. 9); Table 1 on p. 857 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 858 (PDF p. 9)] We simulate 25 million random assignments and, for each of these random assignments, compute the upper bound variance estimates $\hat V_N^a$, $\hat V_N^{b+}$ and $\hat V_N^H$, and associated confidence intervals that would have been obtained. For the collection of 25 million simulations, we calculate the mean variance estimate, the mean width of the associated 95% confidence intervals for $\tau_N$ and the fraction of simulated confidence intervals covering $\tau_N$. […] This hypothesis, denoted 'Sharp Null,' assumes that $y_{0i} = y_{1i}$ for all $i$. Under the Sharp Null, the treatment effect estimator variance is 0.199 USD$^2$. As can be seen in Table 2, Neyman's estimators predictably perform well since they implicitly assume that the outcomes are perfectly correlated: the bias (5) for $\hat V_N^a$ is zero because $\sigma_N^2(y_1) = \sigma_N^2(y_0) = \sigma_N(y_1, y_0)$. Due to the nonlinearity of the square root function, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality implies that $\hat V_N^{b+}$ has nonpositive bias ($-0.007$ USD$^2$). [Table 2, p. 858, block 'Sharp Null (True Var.: 0.199)'; columns: Mean var. estimate; Mean 95% CI width; Coverage for $\tau_N$] Conventional ($\hat V_N^a$): 0.199; 1.747; 95.2%. Neyman upper bound ($\hat V_N^{b+}$): 0.193; 1.724; 94.1%. Sharp upper bound ($\hat V_N^H$): 0.189; 1.703; 93.7%. [Table 1, p. 857 (PDF p. 8), row 'Neyman upper bound ($\hat V_N^{b+}$)'] 0.196; $(-\$1.548, \$0.185)$. [Corrected claim, from Sol's smallest repair] 'Due to the nonlinearity of the square root function, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality implies that $\hat V_N^{b+}$ has nonpositive bias.' The parenthesis '($-0.007$ USD$^2$)' is deleted; a replacement figure needs the original simulation output. [Formal content] (a) [The retained claim; $n = N$ and $y_{0i} = y_{1i}$ for all $i$] $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat V_n^{b+}) \le V_n$. (b) [Any finite collection] For real numbers $v_1, \ldots, v_M \ge 0$ ($M \ge 1$) and real $c$: $\left(\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mc\sqrt{v_j}\right)^2 \le c^2\cdot\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mv_j$. (c) [The multiplier, from Table 1] If $q \ge \frac{391}{2000}$, $0 \le d \le \frac{867}{500}$ and $d^2 = c^2q$, then $c^2 \le \frac{44217}{2875}$. (d) [Incompatibility] There are no real numbers $c$, $\bar w$, $\bar v$, $V$, $b$ with $c^2 \le \frac{44217}{2875}$, $\bar v \ge 0$, $\bar w \ge \frac{3447}{2000}$, $\bar w^2 \le c^2\bar v$, $V \le \frac{399}{2000}$, $b \le -\frac{13}{2000}$ and $\bar v = V + b$. (e) [With the multiplier $c = 3.92$] $\bar w \ge 1.7235$ and $\bar w^2 \le 3.92^2\,\bar v$ give $\bar v \ge \frac{11881809}{61465600} > \frac{193}{1000}$, while $V \le 0.1995$ and $b \le -0.0065$ give $\bar v = V + b \le 0.193$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat V_n^{b+}$ is (6) and $V_n$ is (3), in the standing assumptions; under $y_{0i} = y_{1i}$, $\sigma_n^2(y_1) = \sigma_n^2(y_0) = \sigma_n(y_1, y_0)$. Bias is $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat V) - V$. Reading of the numbers: the quoted bias $b$ is the mean variance estimate $\bar v$ over the simulated assignments minus the true variance $V$, from the same collection of assignments as Table 2; each 95% interval is a Wald interval (Remark 4, p. 857: $\hat\tau_N \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}$) of full width $w_j = c\sqrt{v_j}$ with one multiplier $c = 2z_{.975}$, and $\bar w$ is the mean width. A real number displays as a three-decimal number $p$ if it lies in $[p - \frac{1}{2000}, p + \frac{1}{2000}]$: the true variance 0.199 gives $V \le \frac{399}{2000}$, the bias $-0.007$ gives $b \le -\frac{13}{2000}$, the mean width 1.724 gives $\bar w \ge \frac{3447}{2000}$; in Table 1 the variance 0.196 gives $q \ge \frac{391}{2000}$ and the interval $(-1.548, 0.185)$ gives a full width $d \le 0.1855 + 1.5485 = \frac{867}{500}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) With $A = \hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)$ and $B = \hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)$: $\mathrm{E}_X(A) = \mathrm{E}_X(B) = \sigma_n^2(y_1)$ under the sharp null (p. 852), $\mathrm{E}_X\{(AB)^{1/2}\} \le \{\mathrm{E}_X(A)\mathrm{E}_X(B)\}^{1/2}$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and substitution in (6) and (3). (b) is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for a finite average. (c) $c^2 = d^2/q \le \frac{(867/500)^2}{391/2000} = \frac{44217}{2875}$. (d) $\bar v = V + b \le \frac{193}{1000}$, while $\bar v \ge \bar w^2/c^2 \ge \frac{(3447/2000)^2}{44217/2875} = \frac{30364623}{157216000} > \frac{193}{1000}$. (e) $\frac{1.7235^2}{3.92^2} = \frac{11881809}{61465600}$.
canonical_claim.note: P022-N005 is rated an error, Minor. Like P022-T11 it is a finding about reported numbers whose content is an exact arithmetic impossibility: the quoted bias, the Table 2 row and the Wald construction cannot all be rounded summaries of the same simulations. The validator holds a Lean certificate of (b)–(d) (validate/P022-N005/v1/artifact/check.lean, with lean.out); (a), the claim that remains after the correction, is derived in Section 8 of the derivation and is still to be formalized. Not established: which printed number is wrong, or a unique replacement ($-0.006$ and $-0.005$ are both compatible with the other printed figures). If the parenthesis were instead an independently computed population bias, the contradiction would be probabilistic (the validator bounds the probability below $10^{-10}$), not deterministic. P022-N006 (the missing hat in 'the sampling distribution of $\tau_N$', in the parenthesis that follows on p. 858) is a notational misprint in prose with no mathematical statement to correct, and is not a target.

canonical_claim.location: p. 860 (PDF p. 11); proof on pp. 860–861 (PDF pp. 11–12)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement, from Sol's smallest repair. The second sentence is the added hypothesis; the rest is as printed, except the closing remark on the integers.] LEMMA 2 (corrected). Suppose conditions 1–3 of Proposition 1 hold. Suppose in addition that $G_N(x-) \to G(x-)$ at every discontinuity point $x$ of $G$, and $F_N(x-) \to F(x-)$ at every discontinuity point $x$ of $F$. Then $\sup_y|G(y) - G_N(y)| \to 0$ and $\sup_y|F(y) - F_N(y)| \to 0$. In addition, given $\eta_1, \eta_0 > 0$, there exist two positive integers $K_1(\eta_1)$ and $K_0(\eta_0)$ such that $\limsup_N\left\{N\mathrm{P}\left(\sup_y|G(y) - \hat G_N(y)| \ge \eta_1\right)\right\} \le \frac{(1-\theta\rho)K_1(\eta_1)}{\theta\rho\eta_1^2}$, $\limsup_N\left\{N\mathrm{P}\left(\sup_y|F(y) - \hat F_N(y)| \ge \eta_0\right)\right\} \le \frac{\{1-\theta(1-\rho)\}K_0(\eta_0)}{\theta(1-\rho)\eta_0^2}$. The integers are nonincreasing in $\eta$. [Explicit choice, from the validator] $K_1(\eta) = K_0(\eta) = 2\lceil 4/\min(\eta, 1)\rceil$ is admissible; it does not depend on $H$. [Corrected proof step, p. 861] 'By conditions 2 and 3 and the added hypothesis, this is satisfied for all $N$ sufficiently large.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population, the design, $\mu_N$, $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_N(\cdot,\cdot)$, $\tau_N$, $\hat\tau_N$, $\mathrm{E}_X$, $V_N$ of (2), $\hat\sigma_N^2$, $G_N$, $F_N$ and their left-continuous inverses, (7), $V_N^H$, $V_N^L$, $\hat G_N$, $\hat F_N$, the partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n}$, (8), (9), and for $n = N$ (3), (4), (6) are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. The nested sequence $\{U_N\}_N$, $H_N$, $H$, $G$, $F$, $\theta$, $\rho$ and conditions 1–4 of Proposition 1 are transcribed in the standing assumptions (Section 4, p. 855, PDF p. 6). $G(x-) = \lim_{y \uparrow x} G(y)$ and $G_N(x-) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{1i} < x)$; likewise $F(x-)$, $F_N(x-) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{0i} < x)$, and $\hat G_N(x-)$, $\hat F_N(x-)$ with the sampled units. A discontinuity point of $G$ is an atom of the first marginal of $H$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (i) [Each $N$, each real $y$; exact] $\mathrm{E}_X\hat G_N(y) = G_N(y)$ and $\mathrm{Var}_X\hat G_N(y) = \frac{N-m}{(N-1)m}G_N(y)\{1 - G_N(y)\} \le \frac{N-m}{4(N-1)m}$; the same holds with $y-$ in place of $y$ (indicators $I(y_{1i} < y)$); likewise for $\hat F_N$ with $n - m$ in place of $m$ (this is P022-T4). (ii) [Deterministic] If $P$ and $A$ are distribution functions and $s < t$ satisfy $P(t-) - P(s) \le \delta$, then for all $s \le x < t$: $P(t-) - A(t-) - \delta \le P(x) - A(x) \le P(s) - A(s) + \delta$. (iii) [Deterministic] For a distribution function $P$ and an integer $R \ge 1$, the partition of $[-\infty, \infty]$ formed by $-\infty$, $+\infty$ and the distinct values of $\inf\{y : P(y) \ge j/R\}$, $j = 1, \ldots, R-1$, has at most $R$ intervals, and $P(t-) - P(s) \le 1/R$ for adjacent points $s < t$ (with $P(-\infty) = 0$ and $P(\infty-) = 1$). (iv) [Each $N$] Let $0 < \eta \le 1$, $R = \lceil 4/\eta\rceil$, $P \in \{G, F\}$ with $P_N$, $\hat P_N$ the corresponding population and sampled distribution functions, $k$ the arm size ($m$ or $n - m$), and $b_N$ the largest of $|P(s) - P_N(s)|$ and $|P(t-) - P_N(t-)|$ over the partition points of (iii). If $b_N < \eta/4$, then $\mathrm{P}\left(\sup_y|P(y) - \hat P_N(y)| \ge \eta\right) \le \frac{2R(N-k)}{(N-1)k\eta^2}$ (by (ii), a supremum of at least $\eta$ forces $|\hat P_N - P_N| \ge \eta/2$ at one of at most $2R$ endpoint values; union bound and Chebyshev's inequality with (i)). Multiplying by $N$ and letting $N \to \infty$ with $k/N \to \alpha$ gives $2R(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\eta^2)$, the printed form with $K(\eta) = 2R$, $\alpha = \theta\rho$ for $\hat G_N$ and $\alpha = \theta(1-\rho)$ for $\hat F_N$. (v) For $\eta > 1$ the event $\{\sup_y|P(y) - \hat P_N(y)| \ge \eta\}$ is empty. (vi) [Where the added hypothesis enters] Weak convergence gives $P_N(x) \to P(x)$ and $P_N(x-) \to P(x-)$ at continuity points $x$ of $P$; at a discontinuity point, condition 3 gives $P_N(x) \to P(x)$ and the added hypothesis gives $P_N(x-) \to P(x-)$; so $b_N \to 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, smallest_repair and prior_correction; proof of sufficiency in validate/P022-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, Section 3, and independently in validate/P022-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md, Section 5). The added hypothesis is a regularity condition at the atoms of the limiting marginals, not a typographical fix; it excludes both witnesses of P022-T1 (in A, $G_N(0-) = 1$ while $G(0-) = 0$). It holds trivially when $G$ and $F$ are continuous, and with probability one when the units are independent and identically distributed draws from a superpopulation. It cannot be dropped: $\sup_y|G(y) - G_N(y)| \to 0$ implies $G_N(x-) \to G(x-)$ for every $x$. The printed closing remark that the integers 'depend also on the limiting distribution $H$' is not needed with the explicit choice. Remark 1 (p. 855), which says that condition 3 'is used to establish the functional convergence of $(G_N, F_N)$ to $(G, F)$', is to be revised accordingly. The repair is confined to the lemma: Propositions 1 and 2 keep their printed hypotheses and conclusions through replacement proofs that do not use the lemma (P022-T3, and the finite lemmas of P022-T15 and P022-T16).

canonical_claim.statement: LEMMA 2. Suppose conditions 1–3 of Proposition 1 hold. Then $\sup_y|G(y) - G_N(y)| \to 0$ and $\sup_y|F(y) - F_N(y)| \to 0$. In addition, given $\eta_1, \eta_0 > 0$, there exist two positive integers $K_1(\eta_1)$ and $K_0(\eta_0)$ such that $\limsup_N\left\{N\mathrm{P}\left(\sup_y|G(y) - \hat G_N(y)| \ge \eta_1\right)\right\} \le \frac{(1-\theta\rho)K_1(\eta_1)}{\theta\rho\eta_1^2}$, $\limsup_N\left\{N\mathrm{P}\left(\sup_y|F(y) - \hat F_N(y)| \ge \eta_0\right)\right\} \le \frac{\{1-\theta(1-\rho)\}K_0(\eta_0)}{\theta(1-\rho)\eta_0^2}$. The integers are nonincreasing in $\eta$, and depend also on the limiting distribution $H$ of $(y_1, y_0)$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 2, the steps that apply Lemma 2, corrected (direct bound for bounded outcomes)
canonical_claim.location: pp. 867–869 (PDF pp. 18–20); statement of Proposition 2 on p. 863 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed steps replaced: p. 867 (PDF p. 18)] The fourth inequality follows from Lemma 2 which shows that $\sup_y|G(y) - G_N(y)| = o(1)$ and $\sup_y|F(y) - F_N(y)| = o(1)$. We can now apply the second part of Lemma 2 to bound the probability above. [The same two uses are made in the argument for $\hat V_N^L$, pp. 868–869 (PDF pp. 19–20).] [Corrected statement, from Sol's smallest repair: compare the sampled distribution functions with those of the current population $U_N$ directly, without Lemma 2.] Let $N \ge 4$, $m \ge 2$, $n - m \ge 2$, and suppose $|y_{1i}|, |y_{0i}| \le C < \infty$ for all $i \le N$. Let $c > 0$ be such that $m \ge cN$, $n - m \ge cN$ and $N \ge 2/c$. Put $D_1 = \int_{-C}^{C}|\hat G_N(x) - G_N(x)|\,dx$ and $D_0 = \int_{-C}^{C}|\hat F_N(x) - F_N(x)|\,dx$. Then, for $B \in \{H, L\}$: (a) $\mathrm{E}_X(D_1^2) \le \frac{C^2(N-m)}{(N-1)m} \le \frac{C^2}{cN}$ and $\mathrm{E}_X(D_0^2) \le \frac{C^2\{N-(n-m)\}}{(N-1)(n-m)} \le \frac{C^2}{cN}$, hence $\mathrm{E}_X\{(D_1 + D_0)^2\} \le \frac{4C^2}{cN}$; (b) for every assignment, $N|\hat V_N^B - V_N^B| \le \left(\frac{16}{c} + 8\right)C(D_1 + D_0) + \frac{8C^2}{c^2N}$; (c) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N \ge \frac{16C^2}{c^2\varepsilon}$, $\mathrm{P}\{N|\hat V_N^B - V_N^B| \ge \varepsilon\} \le \frac{16(16/c + 8)^2C^4}{cN\varepsilon^2}$. Consequently, if $(m/N, n/N) \to (\theta\rho, \theta)$ with $\theta \in (0, 1]$ and $\rho \in (0, 1)$ (condition 1 of Proposition 1) and $|y_{1i}|, |y_{0i}| \le C$ for all $i$, then for every $\varepsilon > 0$, every $0 < c < \min\{\theta\rho, \theta(1-\rho)\}$ and $B \in \{H, L\}$, $\limsup_N N\mathrm{P}\{N|\hat V_N^B - V_N^B| \ge \varepsilon\} \le \frac{16(16/c + 8)^2C^4}{c\varepsilon^2}$; that is, $\mathrm{P}\{N|\hat V_N^B - V_N^B| \ge \varepsilon\} = \mathcal{O}(C^4/(N\varepsilon^2))$. Conditions 2 and 3, the limits $G$, $F$, $H$, and Lemma 2 are not used.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population, the design, $\mu_N$, $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_N(\cdot,\cdot)$, $\tau_N$, $\hat\tau_N$, $\mathrm{E}_X$, $V_N$ of (2), $\hat\sigma_N^2$, $G_N$, $F_N$ and their left-continuous inverses, (7), $V_N^H$, $V_N^L$, $\hat G_N$, $\hat F_N$, the partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n}$, (8), (9), and for $n = N$ (3), (4), (6) are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. [Proposition 2, p. 863 (PDF p. 14)] $y_1$ and $y_0$ are bounded: $|y_{1i}|, |y_{0i}| \le C < \infty$ for all $i$. $D_1$ and $D_0$ are the $L^1$ distances between the sampled and population distribution functions of each arm (both functions are $0$ below $-C$ and $1$ from $C$ on).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (i) [Cauchy–Schwarz and the variance of a sampled distribution function] $D_1^2 \le 2C\int_{-C}^{C}\{\hat G_N(x) - G_N(x)\}^2dx$, $\mathrm{E}_X\hat G_N(x) = G_N(x)$ and $\mathrm{Var}_X\hat G_N(x) \le \frac{N-m}{4(N-1)m}$ (P022-T4); likewise for $D_0$ with $n - m$; $(D_1 + D_0)^2 \le 2D_1^2 + 2D_0^2$; $\frac{N-k}{(N-1)k} \le \frac1k \le \frac{1}{cN}$ for an arm of size $k \ge cN$. (ii) [Quantile identity] For distribution functions $A$, $P$ of laws on $[-C, C]$ with left-continuous inverses $q_A$, $q_P$: $\int_0^1|q_A(u) - q_P(u)|\,du = \int_{-C}^{C}|A(x) - P(x)|\,dx$. (iii) Hence, in the arm with index $a \in \{1, 0\}$ and size $k_a$ ($k_1 = m$, $k_0 = n - m$): the mean differs from the population mean by at most $D_a$, the second moment by at most $2CD_a$, and the divisor-$k_a$ variance from $\sigma_N^2$ by at most $4CD_a$; with $c_{aN} = \frac{(N-1)k_a}{N(k_a-1)} \le 2$ and $|c_{aN} - 1| = \frac{N-k_a}{N(k_a-1)} \le \frac{1}{k_a-1}$, $|\hat\sigma_N^2(y_a) - \sigma_N^2(y_a)| \le 8CD_a + \frac{C^2}{k_a-1}$. (iv) $|\hat\sigma_N^B(y_1, y_0) - \sigma_N^B(y_1, y_0)| \le 2C(D_1 + D_0)$ for $B \in \{H, L\}$: the integral of the product of quantile functions changes by at most $C(D_1 + D_0)$ (change one factor, bounded by $C$, at a time; $u \mapsto 1-u$ preserves the $L^1$ distance), and the product of the means by at most $C(D_1 + D_0)$. (v) For $N \ge 2/c$: $k_a - 1 \ge cN/2$, $(N - k_a)/k_a \le 1/c$ and $N/(N-1) \le 2$; substituting (iii) and (iv) in $N(\hat V_N^B - V_N^B) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{N-m}{m}\{\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) - \sigma_N^2(y_1)\} + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\{\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) - \sigma_N^2(y_0)\} + 2\{\hat\sigma_N^B(y_1, y_0) - \sigma_N^B(y_1, y_0)\}\right]$ gives (b). (vi) If $N \ge 16C^2/(c^2\varepsilon)$ then $8C^2/(c^2N) \le \varepsilon/2$, and Markov's inequality applied to $\{(16/c + 8)C(D_1 + D_0)\}^2$ with (a) gives (c).
canonical_claim.note: Second part of Sol's smallest repair of P022-E001 (validated.json: 'In Proposition 2 compare sampled and current-population laws directly; the saved derivation proves $\mathrm{P}\{N|\hat V_N^B - V_N^B| \ge \varepsilon\} = O(C^4/(N\varepsilon^2))$, $B \in \{H, L\}$, without Lemma 2'). The derivation, with these constants ($A = 16/c + 8$, $B = 8/c^2$ there), is validate/P022-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, Section 5; an independent version of the same argument is in validate/_batch/P022-B01/work/derivations.md, under E006. Parts (a)–(c) are exact for each fixed $N$; no independence of the two arms is used (each arm is, marginally, a uniformly random subset of its size). The bound has the form $\mathcal{O}(C^4/(N\varepsilon^2))$ with a constant that depends only on the limiting arm fractions, where Proposition 2 as printed has functions $\kappa_1, \kappa_2, \kappa_3$ of a split $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3 = \varepsilon$ that depend on $H$; it gives the $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$ conclusion of Proposition 2 and of Remark 3 under condition 1 and boundedness alone. If $C = 0$ every quantity vanishes.
